annotations.description: Kimi25 Vorthos has Migratory Route and Sylvan Reclamation available to basic landcycle for {2}, and has Sol Ring (untapped) plus a tapped Forest. Sol Ring produces {C}{C}, which covers the {2} generic cost of basic landcycling. Since they have Kodama's Reach in hand (costs {2}{G}) and need to hit land drops to cast their expensive spells (Realm Seekers, Reverse the Sands, Migratory Route for full cost later), cycling one of these cards to find a basic land would ensure they hit their turn 3 land drop and set up Kodama's Reach on turn 3. Declining to use this mana at end of turn wastes 2 mana from Sol Ring and misses an opportunity to smooth their draws. Both Sylvan Reclamation and Migratory Route are less immediately useful than ensuring consistent land drops in the early game.

annotations.description: With two Forests untapped and both Thought Vessel and Rampant Growth costing 2 mana, casting Rampant Growth would be the better play. Rampant Growth searches for a basic land and puts it onto the battlefield tapped, guaranteeing a 3rd land on turn 3 and enabling the player to cast Forgotten Ancient (4 mana) on turn 3 with the land drop. Thought Vessel provides colorless mana and no-max-hand-size, but with only 7 cards in hand (dropping to 6 after casting), the no-max-hand-size is irrelevant right now. Rampant Growth accelerates mana development more effectively since it adds a land permanently, while Thought Vessel is an artifact that can be destroyed. More importantly, Rampant Growth on turn 2 followed by a land drop on turn 3 gives access to 4 mana on turn 3 (3 lands + the new tapped land from Rampant Growth untapping), enabling Forgotten Ancient. With Thought Vessel instead, turn 3 gives access to only 4 mana as well (2 forests + land drop + Thought Vessel), so the mana count is actually equivalent. However, Rampant Growth thins the deck and provides colored mana, which is more valuable given the player has Rampant Growth, Forgotten Ancient (needs G), and Day of the Dragons (needs UUU) in hand. Getting a third forest or an island via Rampant Growth improves color fixing. Thought Vessel only adds colorless.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Thought Vessel on turn 2 with two Forests.
annotations.betterLine: Cast Rampant Growth to search for an Island (fixing for Day of the Dragons and Synthetic Destiny's blue requirements), providing better color fixing and deck thinning while achieving equivalent mana acceleration.

annotations.description: With only 1 land (Tolaria West, which enters tapped) and no way to play a land this turn, casting Shadowspear (1 mana) vs Commander's Plate (1 mana) is the choice. Shadowspear gives +1/+1, trample, lifelink and has a cheap equip cost of 2, while Commander's Plate gives +3/+3 and protection but has equip 5 (or equip commander 3). With Zndrsplt/Okaun as commanders, Commander's Plate would give protection from all colors except red/blue, which is extremely powerful. However, Shadowspear is more castable and equippable early. The real question is whether Thought Vessel should have been cast instead to help with mana development, since the player has a very expensive hand (Niv-Mizzet at 6 mana, Impulsive Maneuvers at 4, etc.) and only 1 land. But Thought Vessel costs 2 mana and they only have 1 land available, so they can't cast it. Between Shadowspear and Commander's Plate at 1 mana each, Shadowspear is reasonable as it has a cheaper equip cost. However, given that Tribute Mage can tutor for a 2-mana artifact (like Thought Vessel), casting Fabricate to find Sol Ring or another mana rock might have been better - but Fabricate costs 3 mana. With only 1 mana available, the choice is genuinely between Shadowspear and Commander's Plate, and Shadowspear with its cheaper equip cost is defensible.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Shadowspear for 1 mana
annotations.betterLine: Commander's Plate might have been slightly better since it provides protection from white, green, and black (all colors not in Izzet identity) which is incredibly powerful on Okaun, making it nearly unblockable and hard to remove. However, with equip 5 vs Shadowspear's equip 2, this is genuinely debatable given the mana-starved position.

The choices presented were to cycle Sylvan Reclamation or Migratory Route (basic landcycling), but the real miss is that they should have played Command Tower and then cast Kodama's Reach to ramp significantly. The decision point only shows cycling options, but the player's reasoning suggests they chose to do nothing this turn, missing a crucial ramp opportunity on turn 3.
annotations.actionTaken: Declined to cycle Sylvan Reclamation or Migratory Route, apparently doing nothing meaningful on turn 3.

Both are reasonable, but Elvish Rejuvenator is arguably better here because: (1) Libby's commander is Obuun, Mul Daya Ancestor, which cares about landfall and having creatures to put counters on - the 1/1 body is a relevant target, (2) the land from Rejuvenator enters the battlefield triggering future landfall, and (3) Libby already has Boros Guildgate in hand for next turn's land drop. Kodama's Reach gives a land to hand which is slightly redundant when you already have Boros Guildgate. However, Kodama's Reach guarantees finding a specific basic land type and gives card advantage (two cards effectively), so this is genuinely debatable.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Kodama's Reach to search for two basic lands (one to battlefield tapped, one to hand)
annotations.betterLine: Cast Elvish Rejuvenator to get a land onto the battlefield and a creature body that can receive Obuun's +1/+1 counters, since Boros Guildgate already covers the next land drop

annotations.description: With Harrow in hand (which requires sacrificing a land and fetches two basic lands to the battlefield untapped), putting the Forest onto the battlefield and keeping the Plains in hand would be slightly less optimal than putting the Plains onto the battlefield and keeping the Forest in hand. However, looking at the hand more carefully: the player has Boros Guildgate (R/W), Elvish Rejuvenator (2G), Waker of the Wilds (2GG), Emeria Shepherd (5WW), Far Wanderings (2G), and Harrow (2G, sac a land). The player already has Forest, Plains, Mountain on the battlefield. Putting Forest on the battlefield gives them 2 Forest, 1 Plains, 1 Mountain. Keeping Plains in hand means they can play it next turn for a land drop. But putting Plains on the battlefield (2 Forest, 2 Plains, 1 Mountain after the land from Kodama's Reach) and keeping Forest in hand would give better access to white mana for Emeria Shepherd (5WW) in the long run and the Forest could be the land drop next turn. Either way it's close, but with Emeria Shepherd requiring WW and the player only having one Plains, putting the Plains onto the battlefield to have two white sources sooner is marginally better. The difference is small since Harrow can also fetch Plains later.
annotations.actionTaken: Put Forest onto the battlefield tapped, keeping Plains in hand
annotations.betterLine: Put Plains onto the battlefield tapped, keeping Forest in hand, to build toward the WW requirement for Emeria Shepherd and maintain green mana flexibility through the Forest land drop next turn

Missing this ramp opportunity on turn 3 is a clear value loss.

annotations.description: Kimi25 Vorthos declined to basic landcycle Migratory Route or Sylvan Reclamation at end of turn. However, since they already have Command Tower, Forbidden Orchard, and Azorius Chancery in hand, they have plenty of land drops available. Given they have Command Tower + Azorius Chancery providing good color fixing and Kodama's Reach to cast soon, declining is defensible but slightly suboptimal - they could have cycled Migratory Route to get a basic land, since with only 2 mana sources on board, having maximum lands is critical in the early game.

With 4 lands (2 Forests, Command Tower, Sol Ring), they have access to 1G + 1G + any color + CC = 5 mana including GU, which is enough to cast Edric (1GU) with mana to spare. However, playing Forbidden Orchard instead (which enters untapped and taps for any color) would have been strictly better than the tapped Azorius Chancery this turn - it would give immediate mana access without bouncing a land, allowing Edric to be cast AND keeping all existing lands. The Chancery could be played on a later turn when the tempo loss matters less. Playing a tapland that bounces a land on a turn where you want to deploy a 3-mana creature is a tempo loss.

annotations.description: Casting Synthetic Destiny with only one creature (Forgotten Ancient, which has accumulated +1/+1 counters) is extremely poor value. Synthetic Destiny exiles ALL creatures you control and then reveals cards until you find that many creature cards. With only 1 creature, you exile your Forgotten Ancient (losing all its counters) to get exactly 1 random creature from your library. This is a 6-mana spell being used essentially as a terrible gamble to replace one good creature with one random one. Furthermore, Synthetic Destiny is much more powerful when you have many small creatures on board (like token armies), turning them all into the best creatures in your deck. Using it on a single creature wastes the card's primary value proposition. Additionally, Wistful Selkie was available to cast first for 3 mana (drawing a card and adding a second creature to the board), which would have at least given Synthetic Destiny 2 creatures to work with if the plan was to cast it this turn. The player also had Beastmaster Ascension available, which would be a strong proactive play to set up future attacks.

annotations.betterLine: Cast Wistful Selkie first (3 mana, draws a card, adds a body), then if still wanting to cast Synthetic Destiny, at least exile 2 creatures to get 2 back. Better yet, hold Synthetic Destiny for a turn when you have more creatures on board, and instead play Beastmaster Ascension or Wistful Selkie + land drop this turn to build board presence.

annotations.description: Villain declined to activate Oran-Rief, the Vastwood to put a +1/+1 counter on Caller of the Pack (a green creature that entered this turn or could benefit). More importantly, Villain is in the combat phase with Caller of the Pack (8/6 with trample and myriad) on the battlefield. Looking at the board state, Caller of the Pack should be attacking. The decision point is about using instants/abilities during combat - declining to use Oran-Rief is a minor missed opportunity if Caller of the Pack entered this turn (making it 9/7), though Oran-Rief only works on green creatures that entered this turn. If Caller of the Pack didn't enter this turn, Oran-Rief wouldn't work on it. The bigger issue is the confused reasoning - Villain seems to think it's not their turn, but the decision clearly states it's Turn 8 COMBAT for Gem25P Villain. The pass is reasonable if there's nothing meaningful to activate, but Oran-Rief was offered as an option, suggesting it had a valid target.
annotations.actionTaken: Passed without activating Oran-Rief, the Vastwood or casting Synthetic Destiny during their own combat phase.
annotations.betterLine: If Caller of the Pack entered the battlefield this turn, should have tapped Oran-Rief to put a +1/+1 counter on it before damage, making it a 9/7 trampler (and its myriad copies would also be larger). The reasoning was also confused about whose turn it was.

annotations.description: Kimi25 cast Migratory Route (costs 3WU = 5 mana) before playing a land for the turn. They have Jungle Shrine, Forbidden Orchard, and Plains in hand. Playing a land first (like Forbidden Orchard for immediate untapped mana, or Plains) would give them more mana available this turn or set up better for future turns. Additionally, casting creatures/tokens before combat when Edric, Spymaster of Trest is on the battlefield means the Bird tokens could have attacked this turn to draw cards if sequenced properly - but since Migratory Route is a sorcery and the tokens would need haste to attack, that's less relevant. The main issue is not playing a land before casting the spell, losing a potential mana this turn. With the land drop they'd have access to more mana post-Migratory Route for other plays.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Migratory Route without first playing a land for the turn.
annotations.betterLine: Play Forbidden Orchard (or Plains) first for the land drop, then cast Migratory Route. This preserves maximum mana availability and doesn't cost anything.

annotations.description: GPT5m Analyst cast Commander's Plate (a 1-mana equipment that gives +3/+3 and protection from colors not in commander's color identity) before playing Command Tower from hand. This is a sequencing error - they should play the land first to have more mana available. Additionally, Commander's Plate costs 5 to equip to non-commanders (or 3 to equip a commander), and the Analyst has no creatures on board to equip it to. Casting it now accomplishes very little. More importantly, with 4 lands + Izzet Signet available (potentially 5 mana with Command Tower), casting Tribute Mage would have been more impactful - it searches for a 2-mana artifact and puts a body on the board. Alternatively, Sakashima the Impostor (4 mana) could copy an opponent's strong creature like Caller of the Pack. The Commander's Plate with no creature to equip and expensive equip costs is a low-priority play compared to developing the board with Tribute Mage or Sakashima.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Commander's Plate for 1 mana with no creatures on board to equip it to.
annotations.betterLine: Play Command Tower first, then cast Tribute Mage (3 mana) to search for a 2-mana artifact (like getting back a Thought Vessel or finding Sol Ring if available), putting a body on board. Alternatively, cast Sakashima the Impostor copying Caller of the Pack or Edric.

annotations.description: Evolutionary Escalation requires putting three +1/+1 counters on a target creature an opponent controls. Kimi25 chose Skullwinder (a 1/3 with deathtouch) over Caller of the Pack (an 8/6 with trample and myriad). While Skullwinder becomes a 4/6 deathtouch, Caller of the Pack would become 11/9 - but Caller of the Pack is already a massive threat with myriad that creates token copies when attacking. Adding +3/+3 to it makes each myriad copy even larger. However, the Skullwinder with deathtouch growing larger is also problematic as it becomes a better blocker. The better choice would have been to put counters on Caller of the Pack since it's already an 8/6 - the marginal difference between 8/6 and 11/9 is less impactful than turning a 1/3 deathtouch into a 4/6 deathtouch, which is a much more significant relative upgrade for blocking and trading. Actually, you WANT to minimize the benefit to opponents - Caller of the Pack going from 8/6 to 11/9 is less meaningful (it was already huge) than Skullwinder going from 1/3 to 4/6 deathtouch (now a real combat threat). So putting counters on Caller of the Pack would have been better since the marginal impact is smaller on an already-massive creature.
annotations.actionTaken: Put three +1/+1 counters on Skullwinder (1/3 deathtouch becomes 4/6 deathtouch)
annotations.betterLine: Put the counters on Caller of the Pack (8/6 becomes 11/9) since the marginal impact of +3/+3 is less significant on an already enormous creature, while making a deathtouch creature significantly larger gives the opponent a much better blocker/attacker

The Waker is Libby's only creature and a key mana sink for animating lands. Risking it in combat for 3 damage when opponents have larger boards and blockers available gains very little. annotations.description: Evolutionary Escalation puts +1/+1 counters on a creature you control AND a creature an opponent controls. Putting counters on Edric, Spymaster of Trest is suboptimal because Edric's value comes from his triggered ability (drawing cards when creatures deal combat damage to opponents), not from his combat stats. A 1/1 Bird token with flying would benefit much more from +1/+1 counters since it can actually connect for combat damage more reliably thanks to evasion, and growing a flier makes it a real threat. Making Edric bigger just makes him a slightly larger ground body that you don't particularly want to risk in combat anyway, since losing him means losing the card draw engine.
annotations.actionTaken: Put the three +1/+1 counters from Evolutionary Escalation on Edric, Spymaster of Trest.
annotations.betterLine: Put the three +1/+1 counters on one of the Bird tokens with flying, which has evasion and can more effectively leverage the increased power to deal combat damage and trigger Edric's draw ability.

annotations.description: Evolutionary Escalation requires putting +1/+1 counters on an opponent's creature. The three options were Ohran Viper (1/3 deathtouch + combat damage draw), Skullwinder (1/3 deathtouch), and Caller of the Pack (8/6 trample with myriad). Putting counters on Caller of the Pack makes an already-huge creature slightly bigger (11/9), but it already has trample and myriad so the marginal impact of +3/+3 is relatively small compared to buffing a smaller creature. However, Skullwinder also has deathtouch, meaning the +1/+1 counters don't meaningfully improve it as a combat threat since it already kills anything it touches. The real concern is that a 4/6 deathtouch is harder to attack into. Caller of the Pack with myriad creates token copies when attacking, and those copies would also be 11/9 with trample, making it significantly more dangerous in a multiplayer game. Putting counters on Caller of the Pack is arguably the worst choice since it amplifies myriad damage across all opponents, but Skullwinder gaining +3/+3 on a deathtouch body also makes it a more threatening blocker/attacker. This is debatable but Caller of the Pack with myriad multiplying the bonus across multiple combat instances is likely the worse target to avoid.
annotations.actionTaken: Put three +1/+1 counters on Skullwinder (making it a 4/6 deathtouch)
annotations.betterLine: Could arguably put counters on Caller of the Pack since it's already an 8/6 and the marginal +3/+3 matters less on an already-large body, though myriad tokens copying the buffed stats is concerning. Ohran Viper might be the best target since it's a small 1/3 that becomes 4/6 but doesn't have the same board-warping potential as the other two. The decision is genuinely close.

annotations.description: Caller of the Pack is an 8/6 trampler with Myriad that creates token copies attacking each other opponent - it's the most threatening creature on the board by far. Ohran Viper is just a 1/3 deathtouch creature that's much easier to deal with in combat.

annotations.betterLine: Put the bribery counter on Caller of the Pack to prevent the 8/6 trampling myriad creature from attacking, which would deal massive damage across the table every combat.

Discarding a castable, high-impact ramp spell over more expensive or situational cards is a real mistake.

annotations.description: Casting Fabricate to search for an artifact when there's no clear high-impact artifact to find, while Sakashima the Impostor could copy Caller of the Pack (8/6 trample with myriad) for a game-winning threat, or at minimum Tribute Mage provides the same artifact-searching function plus a body to equip Shadowspear/Commander's Plate to.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Fabricate (2U) to search for an artifact with no obvious high-impact target
annotations.betterLine: Cast Sakashima the Impostor (2UU) copying Gem25P's Caller of the Pack to get an 8/6 with trample and myriad, which would be a massive threat especially with equipment available to attach. Alternatively, Tribute Mage gives a body + artifact search at the same cost as Fabricate.

annotations.description: Evolutionary Escalation counters placed on the already-massive Edric (17/17 becoming 20/20) instead of on a Bird Token with flying evasion. The marginal value of +3/+3 on an already huge ground creature is low compared to making a flying Bird Token significantly larger, which would deal more reliable combat damage through evasion and trigger Edric's card draw ability.
annotations.actionTaken: Put three +1/+1 counters on Edric, Spymaster of Trest (already 17/17)
annotations.betterLine: Put the counters on a Bird Token to create a larger flying threat that can reliably get through for combat damage and Edric card draws

annotations.description: GPT5m Analyst is playing a coin-flip themed deck with Zndrsplt/Okaun as commanders. Krark's Thumb is the single most important artifact in the deck - it lets you flip two coins and ignore one for every coin flip, dramatically improving the odds on Okaun's combat trigger, Zndrsplt's card draw, Chance Encounter win condition, and every other coin flip card. Mind Stone is just a mana rock that adds colorless mana, which is far less impactful. The player already has 7 mana sources (Tolaria West, Path of Ancestry, Command Tower, Mountain, Izzet Signet, Commander's Plate doesn't tap for mana, but Shadowspear doesn't either) - they have adequate mana. Krark's Thumb is a legendary artifact that's irreplaceable for the deck's strategy and is the #1 tutor target in a coin-flip deck.
annotations.actionTaken: Fetched Mind Stone with Fabricate
annotations.betterLine: Fetch Krark's Thumb with Fabricate. It's the cornerstone of the coin-flip strategy, enabling Chance Encounter (already in hand) to accumulate luck counters twice as fast, and dramatically powering up Okaun/Zndrsplt combat triggers. This is the signature tutor target for this archetype.

annotations.description: Gem25P Villain is at 6 life and Qwen3L Libby has Waker of the Wilds (3/3) available to attack. With Naya Charm in hand (which can deal 3 damage to a creature or tap all creatures a player controls), Libby could attack with Waker of the Wilds and if it connects deal 3 damage, then follow up with Naya Charm for 3 more damage to finish off the 6-life Villain. Instead, the player's reasoning shows complete confusion about the game state, talking about 'Turn 2' and 'looping' and trying to 'pass_priority' - they appear to have lost track of the actual game state entirely and likely did not attack at all.
annotations.actionTaken: The player appeared confused about the game state, referenced incorrect turn numbers, and attempted to pass priority rather than making meaningful attack decisions.
annotations.betterLine: Attack Gem25P Villain with Waker of the Wilds (3/3). If it connects, that's 3 damage bringing Villain to 3 life. Then in post-combat main phase, cast Naya Charm choosing the 3 damage mode targeting any creature (or better yet, save it - actually Naya Charm deals 3 to a creature, not a player). The correct line is to attack Villain with Waker of the Wilds to pressure the 6-life opponent, and look for ways to close the game against the vulnerable player.

annotations.description: Discarded Planar Outburst (a board wipe) instead of Abzan Falconer (a mediocre 2/3 with slow outlast synergy). In a multiplayer game with threats like Caller of the Pack (8/6 myriad) on the board, having access to a mass removal spell is valuable. While Banishing Light handles one threat, Planar Outburst handles board-wide problems.
annotations.actionTaken: Discarded Planar Outburst
annotations.betterLine: Discard Abzan Falconer, which is the lowest-impact card - a 2/3 with slow outlast that requires counter synergy to provide flying, while keeping Planar Outburst as a powerful catchall board wipe for a multiplayer game.

annotations.description: Qwen3L Libby is being attacked by enormous creatures (14/12 Caller of the Pack, 16/18 Skullwinder, 8/6 Caller of the Pack, etc.) that could deal far more than 30 damage total. Libby has Naya Charm in hand which can tap all creatures target player controls, completely preventing the combat damage. Instead, the player confused themselves into thinking they weren't involved in this combat decision.
annotations.actionTaken: Attempted to pass priority without blocking or using Naya Charm, mistakenly believing they were not the defending player.
annotations.betterLine: Use Naya Charm to tap all of the attacking player's creatures, preventing what appears to be lethal or near-lethal combat damage against Libby's 30 life.
